propositions.text: Section 231(5) of the Criminal Code defines first degree murder when death occurs while committing certain crimes including unlawful confinement.
propositions.quote: Section 231(5) of the Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, provides that murder is first degree murder, irrespective of whether the murder is planned and deliberate, when the victim’s death is caused “while committing or attempting to commit” any of several listed crimes of domination, including hijacking an aircraft, any form of sexual assault, kidnapping, hostage taking, or unlawful confinement.

propositions.text: Whether the appellant murdered the victim while committing unlawful confinement is at issue in this appeal.
propositions.quote: At issue in this appeal is whether the appellant, Darren Sundman, murdered Jordan McLeod “while committing” the offence of unlawful confinement.

paragraphs.summary: The court states that s. 231(5) defines first degree murder when death occurs while committing certain crimes, and the issue is whether the appellant murdered while unlawfully confining.

propositions.text: The appellant and victim were drug dealers with mutual animosity; the appellant confined and assaulted the victim in a moving truck.
propositions.quote: The appellant and Mr. McLeod were drug dealers with a mutual animosity. On the day of Mr. McLeod’s murder, the appellant unlawfully confined him in a moving pickup truck and repeatedly assaulted him by hitting him with a handgun.

propositions.text: The victim escaped by jumping from the truck but was chased and shot by the appellant and accomplices, resulting in his death.
propositions.quote: Mr. McLeod jumped from the truck when it slowed to make a turn but was then chased on foot by the appellant and two accomplices. When Mr. McLeod ran for his life, the appellant shot him at least three times but did not manage to kill him. As he lay wounded, Mr. McLeod was shot and killed at close range by one of the accomplices.

paragraphs.summary: The court describes the facts: appellant confined and assaulted victim, who escaped but was chased and fatally shot by appellant and accomplices.

propositions.text: Trial judge acquitted appellant of first degree murder but convicted him of second degree murder.
propositions.quote: The appellant was acquitted of first degree murder but convicted of second degree murder.

propositions.text: Trial judge found victim escaped confinement by jumping from truck, so murder was not while committing unlawful confinement.
propositions.quote: The trial judge accepted that although Mr. McLeod was unlawfully confined in the truck, he had managed to escape his confinement by jumping from the truck. The trial judge held that the appellant murdered Mr. McLeod but ruled that because of the brief gap in time between when Mr. McLeod was confined in the truck and when he was killed, the appellant did not murder him “while committing” the offence of unlawful confinement.

propositions.text: Murder was second degree because it was not committed while unlawfully confining the victim.
propositions.quote: The murder was thus in the second degree.

paragraphs.summary: The trial judge found the victim escaped confinement before murder, so murder was second degree, not first degree under unlawful confinement.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal allowed Crown's appeal and substituted first degree murder conviction under s. 231(5)(e).
propositions.quote: The Court of Appeal for British Columbia unanimously allowed the Crown’s appeal and substituted a conviction for first degree murder under s. 231(5)(e) of the Criminal Code.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal held victim was still unlawfully confined when he jumped and was chased, making murder and confinement a single transaction.
propositions.quote: The court held that Mr. McLeod was still unlawfully confined when he jumped from the truck and was chased before being killed. The unlawful confinement and the murder were temporally and causally connected, making the entire series of events a single transaction.

propositions.text: Appellant now appeals to this Court as of right.
propositions.quote: The appellant now appeals to this Court as of right.

paragraphs.summary: The Court of Appeal found victim still unlawfully confined during escape and murder, making it first degree; appellant appeals to this Court.

propositions.text: I would dismiss the appeal and find victim was still unlawfully confined when escaping and murdered during confinement.
propositions.quote: I would dismiss the appeal. In my view, Mr. McLeod was still unlawfully confined when he escaped from the truck and ran for his life.

propositions.text: Victim was coercively restrained by violence, fear, and intimidation even outside the truck, deprived of liberty and not free to move.
propositions.quote: Even though Mr. McLeod was not physically restrained outside the truck, he continued to be coercively restrained through violence, fear, and intimidation. He was deprived of his liberty and was not free to move about according to his inclination and desire.

propositions.text: Appellant murdered victim while unlawfully confining him; acts were a continuous sequence forming a single transaction.
propositions.quote: The appellant then murdered him while unlawfully confining him. These two distinct criminal acts were part of a continuous sequence of events forming a single transaction.

propositions.text: The sequence was close in time and involved ongoing domination from truck confinement through escape to murder.
propositions.quote: They were close in time and involved an ongoing domination of Mr. McLeod that began in the truck, continued when he escaped from the truck and ran for his life, and ended with his murder.

propositions.text: Appellant is guilty of first degree murder under s. 231(5)(e).
propositions.quote: The appellant is therefore guilty of first degree murder under s. 231(5)(e) of the Criminal Code.

paragraphs.summary: The court would dismiss the appeal, finding victim was still unlawfully confined during escape and murder, making appellant guilty of first degree murder.

propositions.text: On January 16, 2015, victim was shot and killed near Prince George after assault and unlawful confinement in a pickup truck.
propositions.quote: On January 16, 2015, Mr. McLeod was shot and killed near Prince George, British Columbia, soon after he had been assaulted and unlawfully confined in a pickup truck.

propositions.text: Five people were in the truck: victim, appellant, appellant’s girlfriend, appellant’s brother, and another man; all were drug dealers.
propositions.quote: Five people had been in the truck: Mr. McLeod; the appellant; the appellant’s girlfriend, Staci Stevenson; the appellant’s brother, Kurtis Sundman; and Sebastian Martin. All five were drug dealers in and around Vanderhoof, British Columbia.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the victim was killed after assault and unlawful confinement in a truck with four others, all drug dealers.

propositions.text: Truck was traveling from Vanderhoof to Prince George; victim was front passenger; appellant and brother carried handguns; another man carried shotgun; victim unarmed.
propositions.quote: The truck had been travelling from Vanderhoof to Prince George. Mr. Kurtis Sundman was driving and Mr. McLeod was in the front passenger seat, while the appellant, Ms. Stevenson, and Mr. Martin were in the back. The appellant and Mr. Kurtis Sundman were each carrying a handgun; Mr. Martin was carrying a shotgun. Mr. McLeod was unarmed.

paragraphs.summary: The court describes the truck trip, seating, weapons carried, and victim unarmed.

propositions.text: Conflict arose during trip; appellant angry for multiple reasons including suspected relationship and drug debt.
propositions.quote: During the trip, a conflict arose between the Sundman brothers and Mr. McLeod. The appellant was angry with Mr. McLeod for many reasons: he suspected that Mr. McLeod was having a relationship with Ms. Stevenson; Mr. McLeod was encroaching on the Sundman brothers’ turf by supplying drugs to the Vanderhoof market; the Sundman brothers owed a drug debt to Mr. McLeod and he was pressuring them to repay the debt; and the appellant had seen messages on Mr. McLeod’s phone that had upset him.

propositions.text: Appellant assaulted victim with handgun; victim tried to avoid blows and promised to forgive debt if left alone.
propositions.quote: At one point, the appellant started hitting Mr. McLeod in the head with his handgun. Mr. McLeod tried to avoid the blows and promised to forgive the Sundmans’ drug debt if they left him alone.

propositions.text: Appellant’s brother encouraged assault and drove truck fast to prevent victim from jumping out; taunted victim to jump though realistically impossible.
propositions.quote: Mr. Kurtis Sundman, who shared the appellant’s anger, encouraged the ongoing assault and drove the truck so fast that Mr. McLeod could not jump out. He also taunted Mr. McLeod by telling him to jump out, even though realistically this was impossible.

paragraphs.summary: The court details the conflict, assault, victim's promise, and brother's encouragement and taunting during the trip.

propositions.text: When truck slowed to turn, victim jumped out and tried to escape; truck stopped and appellant yelled to chase victim.
propositions.quote: When the truck slowed to make a turn, Mr. McLeod jumped out of the truck and tried to escape. Mr. Kurtis Sundman immediately stopped the truck, and the appellant yelled “get him, get him”.

propositions.text: Three men left truck armed and chased victim on foot.
propositions.quote: The three men quickly left the truck, each carrying their respective firearms, and chased Mr. McLeod.

paragraphs.summary: The court states victim jumped from truck when it slowed, was chased by three armed men after truck stopped.

propositions.text: Victim tried to escape through snow, ditch, fence towards bush; appellant shot at victim multiple times, hitting him three times but not killing him.
propositions.quote: Mr. McLeod tried desperately to escape. He waded through deep snow, across a shallow ditch and barbed wire fence, towards the bush. The appellant then shot at Mr. McLeod at least four times, hitting him at least three times. Although these shots did not kill Mr. McLeod, they slowed him down and stopped him from escaping.

propositions.text: An accomplice told appellant he had victim, then shot victim twice at close range, killing him almost instantly.
propositions.quote: Mr. Martin said to the appellant something to the effect of, “I got him, boss”, and shot Mr. McLeod twice, once in the torso and once in the face at close range, killing him almost instantly.

paragraphs.summary: The court describes victim's escape attempt, appellant shooting victim multiple times, and accomplice killing victim at close range.

propositions.text: The three men loaded victim's body into truck and hid it in isolated location; police found body about a month later with help of appellant’s girlfriend.
propositions.quote: The three men loaded Mr. McLeod’s body into the truck and drove to an isolated location where they hid his body under foliage. The police found the body about a month later with Ms. Stevenson’s help.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the men hid victim's body, which police found a month later with appellant’s girlfriend's help.

propositions.text: Appellant and two accomplices charged with first degree murder; accomplices convicted of second degree murder and manslaughter; only appellant’s case remains before this Court.
propositions.quote: The appellant and his two accomplices, Mr. Martin and Mr. Kurtis Sundman, were each charged with first degree murder. The accomplices were convicted of second degree murder and manslaughter, respectively. Only the appellant’s case remains before this Court.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes charges and convictions of appellant and accomplices; only appellant’s case is before this Court.

propositions.text: Crown argued appellant guilty of first degree murder as planned and deliberate or because murder occurred while committing unlawful confinement.
propositions.quote: The Crown argued that the appellant was guilty of first degree murder because the murder was planned and deliberate. Alternatively, the Crown argued that, because the appellant murdered Mr. McLeod “while committing” the offence of unlawful confinement, he was guilty of first degree murder under s. 231(5)(e) of the Criminal Code.

propositions.text: Trial judge rejected both Crown arguments, acquitting appellant of first degree murder but convicting him of second degree murder.
propositions.quote: The trial judge rejected both arguments and acquitted the appellant of first degree murder but convicted him of second degree murder.

paragraphs.summary: The trial judge rejected Crown's arguments for first degree murder and convicted appellant of second degree murder.

propositions.text: Trial judge held Crown must prove murder occurred during continuing confinement to convict under s. 231(5)(e).
propositions.quote: The trial judge held that to prove first degree murder under s. 231(5)(e), the Crown had to prove that the appellant murdered Mr. McLeod while he was under “continuing confinement” at the time of his death (para. 289 (CanLII)).

propositions.text: Victim was unlawfully confined and vulnerable in truck but escaped by jumping out; confinement ended before shooting.
propositions.quote: The appellant repeatedly assaulted and unlawfully confined Mr. McLeod in the truck, and Mr. McLeod was still “in a situation of vulnerability” when he escaped from the truck as a “consequence of the manner in which he had been dealt with in the truck” (para. 289). However, because Mr. McLeod “managed to escape his confinement” by jumping from the truck, when “Mr. McLeod was shot, his confinement had ended” (para. 288).

propositions.text: Brief gap between end of confinement and shooting meant no continuing confinement at death; thus no first degree murder under s. 231(5)(e).
propositions.quote: The brief “gap in time” between the end of Mr. McLeod’s unlawful confinement in the truck and the firing of the fatal shots meant that he was not under “continuing confinement” when he was killed (para. 289). The appellant was thus not guilty of first degree murder under s. 231(5)(e) of the Criminal Code.

paragraphs.summary: The trial judge found confinement ended when victim escaped, so no continuing confinement at death, negating first degree murder under s. 231(5)(e).

propositions.text: Court of Appeal allowed Crown’s appeal, set aside second degree murder conviction, and substituted first degree murder conviction under s. 231(5)(e).
propositions.quote: The Court of Appeal unanimously allowed the Crown’s appeal on the acquittal of first degree murder under s. 231(5)(e), set aside the conviction of second degree murder, and substituted a conviction of first degree murder.

paragraphs.summary: The Court of Appeal allowed Crown’s appeal and substituted first degree murder conviction for appellant.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal found trial judge erred by requiring physical restraint in enclosed space for unlawful confinement.
propositions.quote: The Court of Appeal identified two legal errors in the trial decision. First, the trial judge erred in law on the scope of unlawful confinement by requiring that “the victim be physically restrained in an enclosed space” (para. 156).

propositions.text: Unlawful confinement requires intentional deprivation of liberty or restriction of movement without lawful authority and against wishes.
propositions.quote: Unlawful confinement only requires “the intentional deprivation of another person’s liberty or the restriction of that person’s movement in the absence of lawful authority and contrary to the person’s wishes” (para. 153).

propositions.text: Victim was not free to move according to own desire after jumping from truck; confinement did not end upon jumping.
propositions.quote: Even after Mr. McLeod had jumped from the truck he was “in no sense free to move about according to his own inclination and desire” (para. 159). “His confinement did not, as a matter of law, end as soon as he bailed from the truck” (para. 159).

propositions.text: Applying correct legal test, appellant was committing unlawful confinement when he shot victim.
propositions.quote: Applying the trial judge’s undisputed factual findings to the correct legal test for unlawful confinement, the appellant “was committing the offence of unlawful confinement when he shot [Mr.] McLeod” (para. 159).

paragraphs.summary: The Court of Appeal found trial judge erred by requiring physical restraint; victim was still confined after jumping, so appellant was unlawfully confining when shooting.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal found trial judge erred by concluding brief gap between escape and shooting negated murder while committing unlawful confinement.
propositions.quote: Second, according to the Court of Appeal, the trial judge’s “more fundamental legal error” was in concluding that “the momentary gap in time” between when Mr. McLeod jumped from the truck and when the appellant shot him meant that he could not have murdered Mr. McLeod “while committing” the offence of unlawful confinement (para. 163).

propositions.text: R. v. Paré requires unlawful confinement and murder to be part of a single transaction or temporally and causally connected for first degree murder under s. 231(5)(e).
propositions.quote: Such a “narrow approach” to s. 231(5)(e) diverges from this Court’s interpretation in R. v. Paré, [1987] 2 S.C.R. 618, which asks whether the unlawful confinement and murder were part of a single transaction or were temporally and causally connected.

propositions.text: Trial judge failed to give legal effect to factual findings; unlawful confinement and murder were temporally and causally connected forming a single transaction.
propositions.quote: The trial judge erred in law by failing to give legal effect to his factual findings. On the facts found by the trial judge, there was a temporal and causal connection between the unlawful confinement and the murder, making the entire course of conduct a single transaction.

propositions.text: Temporal connection established by brief gap; causal connection by victim’s vulnerability after escape attempt.
propositions.quote: The temporal connection was established because the gap in time between the unlawful confinement and the murder was “brief” or “momentary” (para. 171). The causal connection was established because Mr. McLeod was still in a situation of vulnerability after he jumped from the truck and tried to escape from his attackers (para. 172).

propositions.text: Based on factual findings, appellant was guilty of first degree murder.
propositions.quote: Based on these factual findings, the appellant was guilty of first degree murder.

paragraphs.summary: The Court of Appeal found trial judge erred by ignoring temporal and causal connection between confinement and murder, making appellant guilty of first degree murder.

propositions.text: Relevant Criminal Code provisions define first and second degree murder and unlawful confinement offences.
propositions.quote: The relevant portions of ss. 231 and 279 of the Criminal Code read as follows: Classification of murder 231 (1) Murder is first degree murder or second degree murder. Planned and deliberate murder (2) Murder is first degree murder when it is planned and deliberate. . . . Hijacking, sexual assault or kidnapping (5) Irrespective of whether a murder is planned and deliberate on the part of any person, murder is first degree murder in respect of a person when the death is caused by that person while committing or attempting to commit an offence under one of the following sections: (a) section 76 (hijacking an aircraft); (b) section 271 (sexual assault); (c) section 272 (sexual assault with a weapon, threats to a third party or causing bodily harm); (d) section 273 (aggravated sexual assault); (e) section 279 (kidnapping and forcible confinement); or (f) section 279.1 (hostage taking). . . . Second degree murder (7) All murder that is not first degree murder is second degree murder. . . . Forcible confinement 279 . . . (2) Every one who, without lawful authority, confines, imprisons or forcibly seizes another person is guilty of (a) an indictable offence and liable to imprisonment for a term not exceeding ten years; or (b) an offence punishable on summary conviction.

paragraphs.summary: The court sets out relevant Criminal Code provisions defining first and second degree murder and unlawful confinement.

propositions.text: Appellant argues Court of Appeal had no basis to interfere with trial judge’s finding that unlawful confinement ended when victim escaped, so no first degree murder under s. 231(5)(e).
propositions.quote: The appellant raises two main issues: A. The Court of Appeal had no basis to interfere with the trial judge’s conclusion that Mr. McLeod’s unlawful confinement ended when he escaped from the truck, and thus the appellant did not murder Mr. McLeod “while committing” the offence of unlawful confinement and is not guilty of first degree murder under s. 231(5)(e) of the Criminal Code;

propositions.text: Appellant argues Court of Appeal erred in concluding unlawful confinement and murder formed a single transaction justifying first degree murder conviction under s. 231(5)(e).
propositions.quote: and B. The Court of Appeal erred in concluding that Mr. McLeod’s unlawful confinement in the truck and his murder formed part of a “single transaction” justifying a conviction for first degree murder under s. 231(5)(e).

paragraphs.summary: The appellant argues the Court of Appeal erred in interfering with trial judge’s findings on unlawful confinement ending and single transaction for first degree murder.

propositions.text: Court will review legal principles for unlawful confinement and first degree murder, then apply to this case.
propositions.quote: I will first review the legal principles for unlawful confinement under s. 279(2) of the Criminal Code and first degree murder under s. 231(5). I will then apply those principles to this case.

paragraphs.summary: The court states it will review legal principles and then apply them to the case.

propositions.text: To establish unlawful or forcible confinement under s. 279(2), Crown must prove accused confined another person and confinement was unlawful.
propositions.quote: To establish unlawful or forcible confinement under s. 279(2) of the Criminal Code, the Crown must prove that (1) the accused confined another person; and (2) the confinement was unlawful (R. v. Magoon, 2018 SCC 14, [2018] 1 S.C.R. 309, at para. 64).

propositions.text: Unlawful confinement involves deprivation of liberty by coercive restraint or direction contrary to wishes for significant time.
propositions.quote: At its core, unlawful confinement involves a deprivation of a person’s liberty (R. v. Bottineau, [2006] O.J. No. 1864 (QL), 2006 CarswellOnt 8510 (WL) (S.C.J.), at para. 117, per Watt J. (as he then was), aff’d 2011 ONCA 194, 269 C.C.C. (3d) 227). Unlawful confinement occurs if, for any significant time period, a person is coercively restrained or directed contrary to their wishes, so that they cannot move about according to their own inclination and desire (R. v. Luxton, [1990] 2 S.C.R. 711, at p. 723; R. v. Pritchard, 2008 SCC 59, [2008] 3 S.C.R. 195, at para. 24; Magoon, at para. 64).

propositions.text: Person need not be physically restrained or restricted to a place; restraint can be by violence, fear, intimidation, psychological or other means.
propositions.quote: The person need not be restricted to a particular place or physically restrained (Magoon, at para. 64; R. v. Gratton (1985), 18 C.C.C. (3d) 462 (Ont. C.A.), at pp. 473 and 475, per Cory J.A. (as he then was); R. v. Lemaigre (1987), 56 Sask. R. 300 (C.A.), at para. 3; M. Manning and P. Sankoff, Manning, Mewett & Sankoff: Criminal Law (5th ed. 2015), at p. 1037). The restraint can be through violence, fear, intimidation or psychological or other means (Magoon, at para. 64).

propositions.text: Purpose of confinement is irrelevant to unlawful confinement determination.
propositions.quote: The purpose of the confinement is not relevant (Pritchard, at para. 31; R. v. Kimberley (2001), 56 O.R. (3d) 18 (C.A.), at para. 107; R. v. Johnstone, 2014 ONCA 504, 313 C.C.C. (3d) 34, at para. 45; R. v. Parris, 2013 ONCA 515, 300 C.C.C. (3d) 41, at para. 47).

paragraphs.summary: The court explains unlawful confinement requires confinement and unlawfulness, involves liberty deprivation by coercion, need not be physical, and purpose is irrelevant.

propositions.text: Examples of unlawful confinement include self-locking to avoid attack or being prevented from escaping through a door.
propositions.quote: For example, a person can be unlawfully confined if an accused’s violent acts lead the person to lock themselves in a room to avoid being attacked (Johnstone, at para. 47; K. Roach, Criminal Law (7th ed. 2018), at p. 442, fn. 83), or if the person is prevented from escaping from an apartment through the front door (R. v. Newman, 2016 SCC 7, [2016] 1 S.C.R. 27, at para. 1; Roach, at p. 442, fn. 81).

paragraphs.summary: The court gives examples of unlawful confinement: self-locking to avoid attack or being prevented from escaping an apartment.

propositions.text: First degree murder requires subjective foresight of death and carries life imprisonment with 25-year parole ineligibility.
propositions.quote: First degree murder is the most serious crime in Canadian law and requires the highest level of moral blameworthiness, namely subjective foresight of death (R. v. Arkell, [1990] 2 S.C.R. 695, at p. 703; Luxton, at p. 724). It carries the most severe punishment under the Criminal Code, a sentence of life imprisonment without eligibility for parole for 25 years (s. 745(a); R. v. Russell, 2001 SCC 53, [2001] 2 S.C.R. 804, at para. 46).

propositions.text: Murder not first degree is second degree, punishable by life imprisonment with parole ineligibility between 10 and 25 years.
propositions.quote: Any murder that is not first degree murder is second degree murder (s. 231(7)), which carries a punishment of life imprisonment without eligibility for parole of between 10 and 25 years, at the discretion of the sentencing judge (ss. 745(c) and 745.4).

paragraphs.summary: The court states first degree murder requires subjective foresight and carries life imprisonment with 25-year parole ineligibility; other murders are second degree.

propositions.text: First degree murder is planned and deliberate or committed with specific victims, situations, or enumerated offences under s. 231(4) to (6.2).
propositions.quote: First degree murder is murder that is “planned and deliberate” (s. 231(2) and (3)). Murder is also deemed to be in the first degree, even if not planned and deliberate, if it is committed in connection with specific victims, specific situations, or any of several enumerated offences (s. 231(4) to (6.2)).

propositions.text: Section 231(5) lists offences (hijacking, sexual assault, kidnapping, hostage taking, unlawful confinement) that elevate murder to first degree.
propositions.quote: Section 231(5) lists one such group of underlying offences. It provides that murder is first degree murder when the death of a person is caused “while committing or attempting to commit” any of the offences of hijacking an aircraft, any form of sexual assault, kidnapping, hostage taking, or unlawful confinement.

propositions.text: Section 231(5) applies even if murder victim and victim of underlying offence differ.
propositions.quote: Section 231(5) can apply even if the murder victim and the victim of the enumerated offence are different persons (Russell, at paras. 33 and 43; Manning and Sankoff, at p. 961).

paragraphs.summary: The court explains first degree murder includes planned murder or murder during certain offences listed in s. 231(5), even if victims differ.

propositions.text: Section 231(5) is a sentencing provision reflecting heightened moral blameworthiness, not a substantive offence.
propositions.quote: Section 231(5) does not create a substantive offence. It is essentially a sentencing provision reflecting Parliament’s decision to treat murder in connection with the listed offences as involving a heightened degree of moral blameworthiness or an aggravating circumstance warranting a more severe punishment.

propositions.text: Section 231(5) applies only after murder conviction beyond reasonable doubt.
propositions.quote: Section 231(5) applies only when the offender has been found guilty of murder beyond a reasonable doubt (R. v. Harbottle, [1993] 3 S.C.R. 306, at p. 323; Arkell, at pp. 702-3; Luxton, at p. 720; Paré, at p. 625; Russell, at para. 24; Pritchard, at para. 19).

paragraphs.summary: The court states s. 231(5) is a sentencing provision for murder with heightened blameworthiness, applying only after murder conviction.

propositions.text: This Court has held s. 231(5) is neither arbitrary nor irrational and does not infringe Charter ss. 7, 9, or 12.
propositions.quote: This Court has held that s. 231(5) is neither arbitrary nor irrational and does not infringe ss. 7, 9, or 12 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms (Arkell, at p. 704; Luxton, at pp. 719-25; D. Stuart, Canadian Criminal Law: A Treatise (8th ed. 2020), at p. 234; Manning and Sankoff, at p. 958).

paragraphs.summary: The court finds s. 231(5) is constitutional and does not violate Charter rights.

propositions.text: The offences in s. 231(5) share the organizing principle of illegal domination of victims.
propositions.quote: The organizing principle for the offences listed in s. 231(5) — what they have in common — is that they are all crimes involving the illegal domination of victims.

propositions.text: Murder connected to these crimes of domination warrants first degree murder punishment.
propositions.quote: Parliament has treated murder committed in connection with these crimes of domination as especially serious and as warranting the exceptional punishment for first degree murder (Paré, at p. 633; Luxton, at p. 722; R. v. Nette, 2001 SCC 78, [2001] 3 S.C.R. 488, at para. 62; Pritchard, at paras. 19-20; Magoon, at para. 61).

propositions.text: Illegal domination is not an essential element to prove under s. 231(5) but guides purposive application of the provision.
propositions.quote: Illegal domination is not an essential element to be proved under s. 231(5) but a principle that helps courts apply the provision purposively, so that the law develops in a principled manner (Russell, at para. 43; Kimberley, at para. 104; R. v. Niemi, 2017 ONCA 720, 355 C.C.C. (3d) 344, at para. 62; R. v. Imona-Russell, 2018 ONCA 590, at para. 13 (CanLII); R. v. McGregor, 2019 ONCA 307, 145 O.R. (3d) 641, at paras. 58, 67 and 69-74).

paragraphs.summary: The court explains s. 231(5) offences share illegal domination as organizing principle, guiding purposive application though not an essential element.

propositions.text: The Court rejects a narrow simultaneous interpretation of 'while committing' under s. 231(5) in favour of a broad single transaction test.
propositions.quote: Wilson J. for the Court rejected a narrow and literal interpretation of “while committing” under s. 231(5) that would require the underlying offence and the murder to be committed simultaneously.

propositions.text: The single transaction test asks if the offence and killing form one continuous sequence of events.
propositions.quote: Instead of a “simultaneous” approach to s. 231(5), Wilson J. adopted the broad and purposive “single transaction” approach proposed by Martin J.A. in R. v. Stevens (1984), 11 C.C.C. (3d) 518 (Ont. C.A.), at p. 541, which asks if the listed offence of domination and the killing “all form part of one continuous sequence of events forming a single transaction”.

propositions.text: Continuing illegal domination gives continuity to events culminating in murder, making entire conduct a single transaction.
propositions.quote: Wilson J. held that “it is the continuing illegal domination of the victim which gives continuity to the sequence of events culminating in the murder. The murder represents an exploitation of the position of power created by the underlying crime and makes the entire course of conduct a ‘single transaction’” (p. 633).

propositions.text: Applying the single transaction test, offender in Paré was guilty of first degree murder as assault and killing formed one continuous sequence.
propositions.quote: Applying this test, the offender in Paré was guilty of first degree murder because the indecent assault and the killing formed “part of one continuous sequence of events” constituting “the same transaction” (p. 634).

paragraphs.summary: The court explains the single transaction test under s. 231(5) rejects simultaneity, focusing on continuous sequence of illegal domination culminating in murder.

propositions.text: Harbottle distilled s. 231(5) into five elements: underlying crime, murder, substantial cause, no intervening act, same transaction.
propositions.quote: This Court in Harbottle, at p. 325, distilled s. 231(5) into five elements: (1) [T]he accused was guilty of the underlying crime of domination or of attempting to commit that crime; (2) the accused was guilty of the murder of the victim; (3) the accused participated in the murder in such a manner that he was a substantial cause of the death of the victim; (4) there was no intervening act of another which resulted in the accused no longer being substantially connected to the death of the victim; and (5) the crimes of domination and murder were part of the same transaction; that is to say, the death was caused while committing the offence of domination as part of the same series of events.

propositions.text: Magoon also recognizes these five elements under s. 231(5).
propositions.quote: (See also Magoon, at paras. 17 and 63.)

paragraphs.summary: The court states Harbottle and Magoon identify five elements for s. 231(5): underlying crime, murder, substantial cause, no intervening act, same transaction.

propositions.text: Section 231(5) requires underlying crime of domination, murder, substantial cause, no intervening act, and same transaction.
propositions.quote: Section 231(5) thus requires (1) an underlying crime of domination; (2) murder; (3) substantial cause; (4) no intervening act; and (5) the same transaction (Parris, at para. 45; McGregor, at para. 61).

paragraphs.summary: The court summarizes s. 231(5) requirements as underlying crime, murder, substantial cause, no intervening act, and same transaction.

propositions.text: The Court has applied the single transaction test by asking if underlying offence and murder have close temporal and causal connection.
propositions.quote: In some cases, this Court has applied the “single transaction” test under s. 231(5) by asking whether the underlying offence of domination and the murder have a close “temporal and causal” connection (see Paré, at pp. 629 and 634; Pritchard, at paras. 19, 25, 33-35 and 38; Russell, at paras. 43 and 46-47).

paragraphs.summary: The court notes the single transaction test has been applied by examining close temporal and causal connection between offence and murder.

propositions.text: In other cases, the Court applied single transaction test without expressly inquiring into temporal-causal connection.
propositions.quote: In other cases, this Court has simply applied the “single transaction” test as enunciated by Martin J.A. in Stevens, without expressly inquiring into the presence of a temporal-causal connection (Harbottle, at p. 326; Magoon, at paras. 73-75; see also R. v. Ganton (1992), 77 C.C.C. (3d) 259 (Sask. C.A.), at p. 263; R. v. Johnson and Jensen (1993), 141 A.R. 184 (C.A.), at para. 53; R. v. Plewes, 2000 BCCA 278, 144 C.C.C. (3d) 426, at para. 34; R. v. Westergard (2004), 24 C.R. (6th) 375 (Ont. C.A.), at para. 30; R. v. Mullings, 2014 ONCA 895, 319 C.C.C. (3d) 1, at para. 102).

propositions.text: Canadian Judicial Council’s Model Jury Instructions focus solely on continuous series of events forming a single ongoing transaction.
propositions.quote: Similarly, the Canadian Judicial Council’s Model Jury Instructions on s. 231(5) focus solely on whether the underlying offence and the killing form “a continuous series of events that was a single ongoing transaction” (“Offence 231(5): First Degree Murder in the Commission of Another Offence”, May 2019 (online); see also D. Watt, Watt’s Manual of Criminal Jury Instructions (2nd ed. 2015), at pp. 716 and 719).

paragraphs.summary: The court states some cases apply single transaction test without temporal-causal inquiry; jury instructions focus on continuous series of events.

propositions.text: Temporal connection is usually easy to identify as close timing between offence and murder.
propositions.quote: It is usually easy to identify a “temporal connection” between an underlying offence of domination and a murder: it is when the two criminal acts are committed close together in time.

propositions.text: It can be harder to articulate the causal connection between underlying offence and murder under s. 231(5).
propositions.quote: But it can be harder to articulate the “causal connection” between an underlying offence and a murder.

propositions.text: Causation in homicide has factual and legal aspects; s. 231(5) causal connection involves neither factual nor legal causation.
propositions.quote: Under s. 231(5), however, a “causal connection” involves neither factual nor legal causation.

propositions.text: Grayson v. Wellington Insurance Co. held murder can be 'in the course of' robbery but robbery is context, not cause, of murder.
propositions.quote: As the Court of Appeal for British Columbia remarked in another context, “[o]ne can murder someone ‘in the course of’ committing a robbery, but the robbery is only the context of the murder, not its ‘cause’” (Grayson v. Wellington Insurance Co. (1997), 37 B.C.L.R. (3d) 49, at para. 26, per Newbury J.A.).

paragraphs.summary: The court explains temporal connection is timing proximity; causal connection under s. 231(5) is not factual or legal causation but a different concept.

propositions.text: Causal connection under s. 231(5) is found when offender’s reason for killing arises from unlawful domination of victim.
propositions.quote: Instead, a causal connection has been found under s. 231(5) where the offender’s reason or motivation for the killing arises from, or is linked to, the offender’s unlawful domination of a victim.

propositions.text: In Paré, causal connection found as accused strangled victim to prevent disclosure after indecent assault, forming single transaction.
propositions.quote: In Paré, Wilson J. found a causal connection between the underlying offence and the killing because the accused strangled the victim to death after indecently assaulting him to prevent him from telling his mother about the assault (p. 634; see also Pritchard, at para. 34).

propositions.text: Causal connection also found when murder facilitates crime of domination, e.g., eliminating witness.
propositions.quote: Likewise, a causal connection has been found under s. 231(5) when the murder was committed to facilitate the crime of domination, such as by eliminating a potential witness to the crime (Pritchard, at para. 38; Russell, at paras. 47-48; R. v. Alexis, 2020 ONCA 334, 388 C.C.C. (3d) 226, at para. 18).

propositions.text: Causal connection under s. 231(5) concerns unifying relationship beyond temporal proximity between domination and murder forming single transaction.
propositions.quote: In all cases, a “causal connection” under s. 231(5) concerns whether there is a unifying relationship, beyond mere closeness in time, between the act of illegal domination and the act of murder, so as to constitute a single transaction (see Alexis, at para. 24).

paragraphs.summary: The court explains causal connection under s. 231(5) means killing motivated by unlawful domination, forming a unifying single transaction.

propositions.text: The single transaction test and temporal-causal connection approach are different ways of addressing the same transaction element.
propositions.quote: I do not read this Court’s decisions as suggesting that the “single transaction” test articulated in Stevens and the temporal-causal connection approach involve different inquiries. They are simply different ways of addressing the “same transaction” element.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the single transaction test and temporal-causal connection approach involve the same inquiry.

propositions.text: In Paré, the murder was temporally and causally connected to the underlying offence as part of one continuous sequence forming a single transaction.
propositions.quote: For example, in Paré, at p. 634, Wilson J. concluded that “[t]he murder was temporally and causally connected to the underlying offence. It formed part of one continuous sequence of events. It was part of the same transaction.”

paragraphs.summary: The court cites Paré as example where murder and offence formed one continuous sequence and same transaction.

propositions.text: In Russell, single transaction test and temporal-causal connection approach are used interchangeably.
propositions.quote: Similarly, in Russell, at para. 46, McLachlin C.J. referred to the single transaction test and the temporal-causal connection approach interchangeably.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes Russell uses single transaction and temporal-causal connection approaches interchangeably.

propositions.text: In Pritchard, a close temporal and causative link is required for s. 231(5) to apply; murder and offence occur in a single transaction.
propositions.quote: Lastly, in Pritchard, Binnie J. stated that there must be a “close temporal and causative link” for s. 231(5) to apply (para. 33, quoting Paré, at p. 629). In the same paragraph, he explained that the murder will occur “while committing” a listed offence when the two crimes occur together in the course of a “single transaction”.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Pritchard requires close temporal and causative link and single transaction for s. 231(5) application.

propositions.text: Properly applied, single transaction test and temporal-causal connection approach involve same inquiry and yield same conclusion.
propositions.quote: Accordingly, properly applied, the single transaction test and temporal‑causal connection approach involve the same inquiry and will result in the same conclusion.

propositions.text: Finding a single transaction necessarily implies temporal-causal connection and vice versa.
propositions.quote: When a single transaction is found, there will necessarily be a temporal‑causal connection. Likewise, when a temporal-causal connection is found, there will necessarily be a single transaction.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes the single transaction test and temporal-causal connection approach are equivalent inquiries with the same result.

propositions.text: Underlying offence and killing must be two distinct criminal acts; underlying offence cannot be consumed in the act of killing.
propositions.quote: Finally, this Court has ruled that the underlying offence of domination and the killing must involve two distinct criminal acts (Pritchard, at para. 27, citing Kimberley, at para. 108, per Doherty J.A.; Magoon, at para. 74; see also Manning and Sankoff, at pp. 961-62). The underlying offence cannot be “consumed in the very act of killing”; in other words, the underlying offence and the killing must not be one and the same (Pritchard, at para. 27).

propositions.text: If only one criminal act, offender did not exploit domination with killing; heightened blameworthiness for first degree murder is absent.
propositions.quote: If there is only one criminal act, it cannot be said that the offender exploited the domination inherent in the underlying offence with the act of killing (para. 29). In such cases, the heightened moral blameworthiness required for first degree murder is absent.

paragraphs.summary: The court rules underlying offence and killing must be distinct acts; one act means no exploitation of domination and no first degree murder blameworthiness.

propositions.text: No issue that appellant was guilty of murdering Mr. McLeod though he did not fire fatal shot
propositions.quote: There is no issue before this Court that the appellant was guilty of murdering Mr. McLeod even though he did not fire the fatal shot.

propositions.text: Trial judge found appellant shot Mr. McLeod with lethal intent and hit him at least three times
propositions.quote: The trial judge found that the appellant shot at Mr. McLeod with lethal intent and hit him at least three times.

propositions.text: Parties do not dispute shots were substantial cause of death as they prevented escape before close-range shooting
propositions.quote: The parties do not dispute that these shots were a substantial cause of Mr. McLeod’s death because they prevented him from escaping his captors, before he was shot and killed at close range.

propositions.text: Only dispute is whether murder was first or second degree, turning on unlawful confinement after escape and same transaction
propositions.quote: The only dispute before this Court is whether the murder was in the first or the second degree. This turns on (1) whether Mr. McLeod was still unlawfully confined after he escaped from the truck; and (2) whether the unlawful confinement (inside or outside the truck, or both) and the murder were part of the same transaction.

paragraphs.summary: Court states appellant guilty of murder though not firing fatal shot; dispute is degree of murder based on unlawful confinement and transaction issues.

propositions.text: Trial judge concluded appellant unlawfully confined Mr. McLeod inside truck due to coercive restraint
propositions.quote: The trial judge correctly concluded that the appellant unlawfully confined Mr. McLeod inside the truck because he was “coercively restrained and unable to move about according to his own inclination and desire” (para. 287).

propositions.text: Trial judge erred in law concluding Mr. McLeod escaped confinement by jumping from truck and confinement ended
propositions.quote: He erred in law, however, in concluding that Mr. McLeod “managed to escape his confinement” by jumping from the truck, and that “at the time Mr. McLeod was shot, his confinement had ended” (para. 288).

propositions.text: Physical restraint is sufficient but not necessary to establish unlawful confinement
propositions.quote: However, physical restraint in a particular place is sufficient but not necessary to establish unlawful confinement.

propositions.text: Even if no physical restraint outside truck, Mr. McLeod remained coercively restrained by violence, fear, intimidation while running
propositions.quote: Even if Mr. McLeod were no longer physically restrained outside the truck, he remained coercively restrained through acts of violence, fear, and intimidation as he ran for his life.

propositions.text: Mr. McLeod continued deprived of liberty and could not move according to his own desire
propositions.quote: He continued to be deprived of his liberty and could not move about according to his inclination and desire.

propositions.text: Crown counsel argued if free, Mr. McLeod would have sought shelter and transport instead of running through snow at night
propositions.quote: Crown counsel made this point vividly during oral argument before this Court: If Mr. McLeod was free to move about according to his own inclination and desire, the [Crown] would hazard to guess that instead of running through deep snow, cutting across fences, poorly dressed in the dead of night in rural Prince George, he would have instead sought out the nearest house, sought some shelter and tried to arrange transport back to his rental car in Vanderhoof.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds trial judge erred in law by concluding confinement ended after escape; unlawful confinement can exist without physical restraint, supported by Crown argument.

propositions.text: Trial judge recognized Mr. McLeod’s continuing vulnerability due to treatment in truck
propositions.quote: The trial judge himself recognized Mr. McLeod’s continuing loss of liberty, finding that “Mr. McLeod was still in a situation of vulnerability, and that vulnerability was the consequence of the manner in which he had been dealt with in the truck” (para. 289).

paragraphs.summary: Trial judge found Mr. McLeod remained vulnerable due to treatment in truck.

propositions.text: Appellant claims analysis precluded because it is not a question of law alone and is a new theory of liability on appeal
propositions.quote: The appellant claims that this line of analysis was precluded before the Court of Appeal and this Court, because it (1) does not involve a question of law alone and (2) is a new theory of liability on appeal.

propositions.text: Rejects both claims by appellant
propositions.quote: I would reject both claims.

paragraphs.summary: Appellant claims analysis precluded as not pure law and new theory; court rejects both claims.

propositions.text: Trial judge’s conclusion that confinement ended outside truck is mixed fact and law, but Crown’s appeal raises question of law alone
propositions.quote: I do not accept that the trial judge’s conclusion that Mr. McLeod was no longer unlawfully confined outside the truck is a question of mixed fact and law, falling outside the Crown’s right of appeal to the Court of Appeal on “a question of law alone” under s. 676(1)(a) of the Criminal Code.

propositions.text: Crown’s appeal challenged legal effect of trial judge’s findings and misapprehension of law on unlawful confinement
propositions.quote: The Crown’s appeal did not challenge the trial judge’s findings of fact or raise a question of how to weigh the evidence and assess whether it meets the standard of proof. Rather, it challenged the legal effect of the trial judge’s findings of fact and his misapprehension of the law relating to unlawful confinement, both of which involve “a question of law alone” falling within the Crown’s right of appeal (R. v. Chung, 2020 SCC 8, [2020] 1 S.C.R. 405, at paras. 10-11; R. v. J.M.H., 2011 SCC 45, [2011] 3 S.C.R. 197, at paras. 28-30).

propositions.text: Trial judge erred in law by requiring physical restraint and enclosure for unlawful confinement
propositions.quote: The trial judge erred in law by viewing unlawful confinement as requiring (1) physical restraint and (2) that the physical restraint be in an enclosed space. As a matter of law, neither element is required.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds trial judge erred legally by requiring physical restraint and enclosure; Crown’s appeal raises question of law alone.

propositions.text: Rejects appellant’s claim that unlawful confinement after escape was new theory not advanced at trial
propositions.quote: I reject the appellant’s assertion that whether Mr. McLeod remained unlawfully confined after he escaped from the truck was a new theory of liability that was not advanced at trial.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal accepted Crown’s closing submission that murder was committed in course of unlawful confinement
propositions.quote: Like the Court of Appeal (at paras. 134-38), I accept that the Crown’s closing submission urged that “the murder was committed in the course of an unlawful conf[inement]” (A.R., vol. III, at p. 60; see also p. 61 (“a murder in the course of an unlawful confinement”)).

propositions.text: Theory of unlawful confinement outside truck was properly raised at trial
propositions.quote: The theory of unlawful confinement outside the truck was thus properly raised at trial.

paragraphs.summary: Court rejects appellant’s claim of new theory; Crown’s unlawful confinement theory was properly raised at trial.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal correctly held Mr. McLeod remained unlawfully confined after escaping truck
propositions.quote: As a result, the Court of Appeal correctly held that Mr. McLeod remained unlawfully confined after he escaped from the truck.

paragraphs.summary: Court affirms Court of Appeal’s holding that Mr. McLeod remained unlawfully confined after escape.

propositions.text: Remaining issue is whether murder occurred while committing unlawful confinement, i.e. part of same transaction
propositions.quote: The remaining issue is whether the appellant murdered Mr. McLeod “while committing” the offence of unlawful confinement; that is, whether these two criminal acts were part of the same transaction.

paragraphs.summary: Court states remaining issue is whether murder and unlawful confinement were part of same transaction.

propositions.text: Appellant murdered Mr. McLeod while committing unlawful confinement as part of one continuous transaction
propositions.quote: Like the Court of Appeal (at paras. 173-74), I have no difficulty concluding that the appellant murdered Mr. McLeod “while committing” the offence of unlawful confinement. The unlawful confinement and the murder were part of one continuous sequence of events forming a single transaction.

propositions.text: Unlawful confinement and murder were close in time; Mr. McLeod still unlawfully confined at death
propositions.quote: The unlawful confinement and the murder were close in time — in fact, Mr. McLeod was still unlawfully confined at the time of his death.

propositions.text: Unlawful confinement and murder involved ongoing domination by intimidation, fear, violence from truck to murder
propositions.quote: The unlawful confinement and the murder also involved an ongoing course of domination consisting of intimidation, fear, and violence. The course of domination started in the truck, continued when Mr. McLeod jumped from the moving truck and was chased by the appellant and his accomplices, and ended with his murder.

propositions.text: Unlawful confinement and murder were distinct acts; confinement not consumed by shooting
propositions.quote: The two criminal acts were also distinct: the unlawful confinement — including the restriction of Mr. McLeod’s freedom of movement inside and outside the truck and the ongoing acts of violence, fear, and intimidation — was distinct from and not consumed by the shooting.

propositions.text: These findings justify verdict of first degree murder
propositions.quote: These conclusions amply justified a verdict of first degree murder.

paragraphs.summary: Court concludes murder and unlawful confinement were one continuous transaction, distinct acts, justifying first degree murder verdict.

propositions.text: Not necessary to apply temporal-causal connection approach as single transaction finding suffices
propositions.quote: In view of this conclusion, it is not necessary to also apply the temporal‑causal connection approach, as the finding of a single transaction necessarily means that a temporal-causal connection is established.

propositions.text: Temporal-causal connection inquiry also supports conclusion: unlawful confinement and murder connected temporally and causally
propositions.quote: In any event, the temporal‑causal connection inquiry yields the same conclusion. The unlawful confinement and the murder were connected temporally because Mr. McLeod was unlawfully confined shortly before and at the time of his death. They were also connected causally, by sharing a unifying relationship, because the appellant murdered Mr. McLeod as he was trying to escape from his unlawful confinement.

propositions.text: First degree murder verdict justified on close temporal-causal connection between unlawful confinement and murder
propositions.quote: The first degree murder verdict was thus justified on the basis of the close temporal-causal connection between the unlawful confinement and the murder.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds temporal-causal connection approach unnecessary but also supports first degree murder verdict.

propositions.text: Appellant contends temporal-causal connection is question of fact, barring Crown’s appeal right
propositions.quote: I would reject the appellant’s contention that whether the unlawful confinement and the murder of Mr. McLeod were temporally and causally connected is a question of fact from which the Crown had no right of appeal to the Court of Appeal.

propositions.text: Court agrees with Court of Appeal that trial judge erred in law by requiring simultaneity of unlawful confinement and murder
propositions.quote: Like the Court of Appeal (at paras. 169-75), I conclude that the trial judge erred in law by concluding that the “brief . . . gap in time” between the unlawful confinement in the truck and the murder precluded these criminal acts being part of the same transaction.

propositions.text: Court has consistently rejected view that unlawful confinement and murder must be simultaneous since Paré
propositions.quote: The trial judge erroneously insisted that the unlawful confinement and the murder must be simultaneous, a view that this Court has consistently rejected since Paré.

paragraphs.summary: Court rejects appellant’s claim that temporal-causal connection is factual; trial judge erred legally by requiring simultaneity.

propositions.text: Even if unlawful confinement ended after escape, trial judge should have considered if confinement and murder formed single transaction
propositions.quote: Further, as the Court of Appeal held (at para. 169), even had the trial judge been correct that the unlawful confinement ended once Mr. McLeod jumped from the truck, the trial judge should have considered whether that unlawful confinement and the murder formed a single transaction.

propositions.text: Unlawful confinement and murder undoubtedly formed single transaction
propositions.quote: For the reasons already stated, they undoubtedly did.

paragraphs.summary: Court agrees trial judge should have considered single transaction even if confinement ended; concludes they formed single transaction.

propositions.text: If appellant had killed Mr. McLeod while confined in truck, murder would be first degree
propositions.quote: if the appellant had shot and killed Mr. McLeod when he was unlawfully confined in the truck, the appellant would unquestionably be found to have murdered Mr. McLeod “while committing” the offence of unlawful confinement.

propositions.text: Mr. McLeod’s brief escape cannot mitigate appellant’s crime or moral blameworthiness
propositions.quote: Mr. McLeod’s brief escape from the truck cannot mitigate the appellant’s crime. On any sensible view, the appellant’s moral blameworthiness cannot be considered to be lower simply because Mr. McLeod managed to jump from a moving truck and was running for his life when he was executed just moments later.

propositions.text: Appellant’s moral blameworthiness equally high in both cases, deserving societal denunciation
propositions.quote: In both cases, the appellant’s moral blameworthiness is exceptionally high; in both cases, it is equally deserving of “a societal denunciation of those offenders who choose to exploit their position of dominance and power to the point of murder” (Luxton, at p. 723).

paragraphs.summary: Court states brief escape does not lessen appellant’s moral blameworthiness; first degree murder verdict justified.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal correctly found appellant guilty of first degree murder under s. 231(5)(e) Criminal Code
propositions.quote: The Court of Appeal was thus correct in finding the appellant guilty of first degree murder under s. 231(5)(e) of the Criminal Code.

paragraphs.summary: Court affirms Court of Appeal’s first degree murder finding under Criminal Code.

propositions.text: Dismisses appeal
propositions.quote: I would dismiss the appeal. Appeal dismissed.

propositions.text: Lists solicitors for appellant and respondent
propositions.quote: Solicitors for the appellant: Pringle Chivers Sparks Teskey, Vancouver; Martland & Saulnier, Vancouver. Solicitor for the respondent: Attorney General of British Columbia, Vancouver.

paragraphs.summary: Court dismisses appeal and lists solicitors for parties.
